title: H-1B Scrutiny Must Not Hurt US Innovation, Indian Diaspora Group Says
excerpt: The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies welcomed the Trump administration's tighter H-1B oversight but warned against a crackdown that chokes the skilled-talent pipeline American industry depends on.
body:
• The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS) welcomed tighter scrutiny of H-1B visa applications, while cautioning that it should not come at the cost of American innovation.
  • FIIDS said employers in fields like artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and advanced semiconductors face highly specific skills gaps that cannot always be filled immediately from the domestic labour pool.
  • The statement from FIIDS policy chief Khanderao Kand came hours after US President Donald Trump tightened oversight of the programme, arguing it had been widely misused by employers including IT outsourcing firms.
  • Kand called for a transparent, enforceable, merit-based system: anti-fraud enforcement, wage safeguards, investment in domestic training, and a lawful, predictable avenue for global talent where a documented need remains.

WASHINGTON — The Foundation for India and Indian Diaspora Studies (FIIDS) on Friday welcomed tighter scrutiny of H-1B visa applications but warned that the crackdown should not come at the cost of American innovation, arguing that jobs requiring highly specialised skills cannot always be filled immediately from the available domestic labour pool.

The statement from FIIDS, an Indian diaspora advocacy group, came hours after US President Donald Trump tightened oversight of the H-1B visa programme, contending that it had been widely misused by certain employers, including IT outsourcing firms.

"FIIDS appreciates and understands the Administration's intent to protect America's national and economic interests, safeguard American workers, and address abuse of the H-1B program. Those are legitimate objectives," Khanderao Kand, Chief of Policy and Strategy at FIIDS, said in a statement on Friday.

A volatile year for the H-1B

The H-1B is a non-immigrant visa that allows US companies to employ foreign workers in specialty occupations requiring theoretical or technical expertise. Technology companies depend on it to hire tens of thousands of employees each year from countries such as India and China, with India accounting for more than 70% of approved beneficiaries, according to industry data.

The programme has been in near-constant flux. In September 2025, the administration introduced a $100,000 fee per H-1B application, which drew sharp pushback from employers and universities. On June 8 this year, a Massachusetts federal court struck the fee down, ruling it unlawful because it lacked congressional approval — a decision diaspora groups including FIIDS and Indiaspora hailed as restoring predictability and fairness to the employment-based immigration system.

"All stakeholders connected with H-1B visas will heave a sigh of relief after the court order, but one wonders if this is truly the end of the matter," Sanjeev Joshipura, Executive Director of Indiaspora, told PTI at the time, cautioning that further procedural hurdles could still emerge.

The skills-gap argument

Kand's core argument is that scrutiny and openness are not opposites: the United States can police abuse while preserving the talent pipeline that powers its technology sector. The ability of the US to attract exceptional talent, he said, is what made it the world's leading innovation economy.

"In fields such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, advanced semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, and specialised data engineering, employers can face real and highly specific skills gaps that cannot always be filled immediately from the available domestic labour pool," Kand said.

He added that the US is strongest when it protects workers from exploitation and discrimination, rewards employers that comply with the law, invests seriously in American talent, and remains capable of attracting the people whose ideas, enterprises and expertise create the next generation of American jobs.

"The answer is not to pit American workers against high-skilled immigrants. The answer is a transparent, enforceable, merit-based system: rigorous anti-fraud enforcement; meaningful consequences for bad actors; strong wage and recruitment safeguards; substantial investment in domestic education, training, and reskilling; and a lawful, predictable avenue for employers to hire global talent when a documented specialized need remains."

— Khanderao Kand, Chief of Policy and Strategy, FIIDS

What is at stake for the diaspora

With India accounting for the overwhelming share of H-1B beneficiaries, the programme's rules directly shape the careers, mobility and long-term plans of hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals and their families in the United States. Tighter oversight could mean longer processing times and more intensive documentation for legitimate applicants — a trade-off FIIDS is urging Washington to manage carefully.

What to watch

The next signals will be in the enforcement mechanics: how scrutiny is applied in practice, whether wage and recruitment safeguards are tightened alongside it, and whether the administration leans on procedural hurdles of the kind Joshipura warned about. For now, FIIDS has positioned itself as neither an opponent of reform nor a defender of the status quo — backing enforcement against bad actors while insisting the system's legal, predictable core survives.
